QuietBuzz needs three permissions to work. Here\'s exactly why.
This is what lets QuietBuzz read and adjust other apps\' notification settings -- specifically, lowering a channel\'s importance so it stays silent instead of turning notifications off entirely.

Android only allows an app to change another app\'s notification settings if it\'s either the single system-wide Notification Assistant, or paired with a device through CompanionDeviceManager. QuietBuzz uses the second option. Linking with any nearby device (Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, either works) satisfies this -- nothing about that device is used afterward. It\'s a permission token, not a connection. Prefer a device you personally own (phone, earbuds, watch, laptop) over shared or office equipment -- for some device types this flow can trigger real Bluetooth bonding as a side effect, which would leave a paired-device record on that equipment tied to your phone.
So QuietBuzz can alert you if the linked device\'s permission is ever revoked and it needs to be re-linked.
Notification access and a linked device are required to continue.

For every app (allowlisted or not), raises LOW categories to DEFAULT, turns vibration back on, and gives categories with no sound the default notification sound. Categories you turned off, and custom ringtones, are left alone. The backup is then cleared.

Some categories are quiet on purpose (music playback, download progress). They'll be raised too and may start making sound; fix those by hand.

Afterwards, tap Run now to turn vibration off again.

Samsung\'s app-level \"Sound and vibration\" switch has no API, so QuietBuzz can\'t change it or keep it in sync. Tap Settings on an app to open its notification page and flip it yourself.
